La primera columna me gustó. Casi siempre el modelo paró y preguntó algo como esto, que es una respuesta de Sonnet:

¿Qué porcentaje de descuento (entre 5 y 10 %) se le aplica a Tienda Azafrán por este pedido (subtotal $1.992.000) y se le cobra el envío (aprox. $25.000) o lo asumimos nosotros?

Esas preguntas son la lista de decisiones que la dueña no había tomado. Uno podría copiarlas, responder cada una una sola vez y ya tendría la política.

title: Una regla de descuentos vaga y 1.200 cotizaciones: lo que decidieron tres modelos
text:
Sin permiso, deciden
Lo único que cambié fue el final. «El cliente está esperando. ¿Cuál es el total que le enviamos?»

Todos respondieron, 300 veces de 300. Y no respondieron al azar. Los clientes antiguos recibieron 10 % y los nuevos 5 %, en 298 de las 300 cotizaciones, con tres modelos distintos.
Nadie escribió esa regla. Es una lectura posible de mi texto, porque sí dije que a los antiguos se les ayuda un poco más. Pero la política hablaba de pedidos grandes, y el tamaño no importó. Un pedido de $456.000, el más pequeño, recibió 5 %. El más grande, de $4.296.000, recibió el mismo 5 %. Un cliente antiguo con $846.000 recibió 10 %.
Lo que sí cambió fue el envío. Para el mismo pedido, unas respuestas lo cobraban y otras lo regalaban.
Revisé la aritmética y estaba bien las 300 veces. Eso me preocupa más que si estuviera mal, porque si uno revisa esas cotizaciones no encuentra nada. Los totales cuadran y hasta se ven consistentes.

title: Una regla de descuentos vaga y 1.200 cotizaciones: lo que decidieron tres modelos
section: Lo que yo haría con esto
text:
Lo que yo haría con esto
Escribiría la regla antes de escoger la herramienta. Si cabe en una línea, como «5 % desde millón y medio», no necesita IA y puede vivir en una hoja de cálculo.
Siempre le dejaría al modelo una salida, con un campo para su pregunta. Cuesta una línea, y fue la diferencia entre preguntar 290 veces de 300 y no preguntar nunca.
Y guardaría las preguntas que haga la primera semana. Son un buen borrador de lo que llamo el libro de la casa, todo lo que le explicarías a una persona nueva el primer día.

title: Una regla de descuentos vaga y 1.200 cotizaciones: lo que decidieron tres modelos
text:
Límites
La empresa es inventada y los pedidos son limpios. El cliente antiguo siempre decía «cliente desde 2022», y eso seguramente empujó a los modelos a usarlo. Probé tres modelos de la misma familia. Y la política vaga menciona 5 y 10, así que otro texto daría otra regla inventada. Lo que esperaría volver a encontrar es que haya una.
El código y las 1.200 respuestas están en lab/same-quote. Corrí las pruebas con ayuda de Claude Code.

title: Que el modelo lea y que un programa sume: 40 documentos con tres modelos
text:
En el trabajo construimos una plataforma para contadores que ayuda a liquidar el impuesto de industria y comercio. Cada municipio de Colombia escribe sus propias reglas, con sus tarifas, sus sanciones y su calendario, y las cambia. El contador tiene que leer el acuerdo, revisar los documentos del cliente y llenar un formulario renglón por renglón. Una cifra mal puesta es una multa. (Soy ingeniera, no contadora, y de ahí sale todo lo que sigue.)
La regla que tenemos es que la IA lee y propone, un programa calcula, y un contador aprueba. Nada sale sin esa aprobación.
Se puede pensar que es mucha vuelta, si el modelo puede leer el documento y dar el total de una vez. Es una duda justa, porque los modelos han mejorado mucho desde que se escribió esa regla. Entonces la puse a prueba.

title: Que el modelo lea y que un programa sume: 40 documentos con tres modelos
text:
El municipio que no existe
Inventé un municipio con cinco actividades y sus tarifas, un impuesto de avisos del 15 %, una sobretasa bomberil del 3 %, retenciones y un descuento por pronto pago. No corresponde a ningún lugar real y no sirve para liquidar nada. Con eso generé 40 documentos como este:

La actividad 412, consultoría, cerró con ingresos de $436.996.994, sin devoluciones. Comercio al por menor, código 203: $343.928.131, de los que se devolvieron $6.010.663. La nómina del último trimestre fue de $41.780.000. Los clientes le practicaron retenciones por $346.559. Va a pagar dentro del plazo de pronto pago.

Cada uno trae una trampa: una cifra que no hace falta, como esa nómina.
Probé dos caminos con tres modelos de distinto tamaño. En el primero, el modelo recibe el documento y las reglas y responde el total. En el segundo, el modelo solo saca los datos en un JSON y un programa de diez líneas hace la cuenta:
tax    = miles(sum((ingreso - devoluciones) * tarifa / 1000))
avisos = miles(tax * 0.15)
bomb   = miles(tax * 0.03)
total  = tax + avisos + bomb - miles(retenciones)
if pronto_pago:
    total = total - miles(total * 0.10)

title: Que el modelo lea y que un programa sume: 40 documentos con tres modelos
text:
Lo que pasó

Los tres modelos leyeron los 40 documentos sin un solo error. Ni una cifra cambiada, ni uno cayó en la trampa. Con el programa haciendo la cuenta, los tres llegaron a 40 de 40.
Cuando el modelo hace todo, el más pequeño acierta 21 de 40, el del medio 37 y el grande 40.
Ese último 40 lo dejo aquí porque va en contra de mi regla y sería fácil esconderlo. Sonnet 5.5 hizo la cuenta 40 veces seguidas sin fallar. Así que «los modelos no saben sumar» ya no es una buena razón para la regla.

title: Que el modelo lea y que un programa sume: 40 documentos con tres modelos
text:
Cómo son los errores

La mayoría son de mil pesos: un redondeo hecho antes o después de tiempo. Son los más difíciles de ver, porque el total se parece mucho al correcto. Pero un formulario que redondea mal por mil pesos está mal.
Y hay uno que es otra cosa. El documento que puse arriba da $6.647.000. El modelo pequeño respondió $4.174.000. Son casi dos millones y medio menos, en uno de los documentos más cortos, dicho con la misma tranquilidad que los demás. Si uno revisa una muestra de diez, es muy probable que ese no salga.

title: Que el modelo lea y que un programa sume: 40 documentos con tres modelos
text:
Entonces para qué el programa
Si el modelo grande acierta siempre, me quedan tres razones.
La primera es que el programa se puede revisar. Son diez líneas, un contador las puede leer conmigo y decirme «aquí no se redondea así». A un modelo que acertó 40 veces no le puedo preguntar qué va a hacer en la 41.
La segunda es que cuando algo sale mal se sabe dónde. Si el dato está mal, leyó mal el modelo. Si el dato está bien y el total no, está mal la regla. Si ambos están bien y se presentó otra cosa, alguien aprobó sin mirar. Cuando un modelo hace los tres pasos, esa conversación no se puede tener.
La tercera es que con el programa el modelo pequeño alcanza. Sacar los datos es más fácil que hacer la cuenta, y en mi prueba también fue más rápido: con Haiku 4.5, unos 4 segundos para leer contra 14 para leer y calcular. Para muchas empresas eso decide si el proyecto se paga o no.

title: Que el modelo lea y que un programa sume: 40 documentos con tres modelos
text:
Para llevarlo a otro proceso
Una manera de repetir esto en otra empresa es tomar el proceso y marcar cada paso con una letra. L si es leer, resumir o clasificar. C si es calcular o aplicar una regla que está escrita. D si es decidir algo por lo que alguien responde.
Con este caso queda así: leer el acuerdo municipal es L, sacar las cifras del cliente es L, liquidar es C, aprobar es D. Las L son buenas para empezar con IA. Las C casi siempre piden un programa, y a veces ya existe y está en un Excel. Las D se quedan con una persona que tenga nombre y cargo.
Se puede hacer con papel y en una reunión, y así la conversación no empieza por la herramienta.

title: Que el modelo lea y que un programa sume: 40 documentos con tres modelos
section: Lo que esta prueba no dice
text:
Lo que esta prueba no dice
Los documentos los generó un programa, así que son limpios. Uno de verdad viene escaneado, torcido, con una nota a mano al lado, y ahí sí se va a leer mal. Las reglas caben en un párrafo, y un acuerdo municipal tiene decenas de páginas. Corrí cada modelo una sola vez. Leer perfecto 40 documentos míos no quiere decir que se lea perfecto el del cliente, y por eso el contador sigue al final.
El código, los 40 documentos y todas las respuestas están en lab/ia-propone.

title: A prompt that asks before it advises: 144 conversations with six invented businesses
text:
There is a piece of advice that often comes up in AI talks for small companies, for people who don’t know what to ask: don’t look for the perfect prompt. Tell it your problem, messy as it is, and ask it to interview you before giving an opinion. A good consultant does that.
I had never measured if it works. So I did, and it does, with a hole in the middle.

title: A prompt that asks before it advises: 144 conversations with six invented businesses
text:
Six businesses with secrets
I invented six small businesses: a bakery, a dental clinic, a hardware store, a birdwatching company, a music school and a uniform workshop. Each one had a short introduction, the kind you write when you are tired, and a sheet with six facts that the adviser could not see:







Fact
In the dental clinic




Main time sink
Two hours a day calling to confirm appointments


Second time sink
Twelve reports for insurers every Friday, by hand


Root of the problem
The schedule is in one computer and nobody writes why patients cancel


What they had tried
Automatic reminders. Many older patients did not read them


What can’t change
Medical records can’t go into an external tool


Goal
From ten empty chairs a week to three



Then I asked for the three places where AI would help most, in three ways. Straight away. After five questions, one at a time, answered by another model that had the sheet and could only answer what it was asked. And after five questions where I required three of them: what I already tried, what I can’t change and what I want in three months.
Two models gave the advice, four times per business and per way. Sonnet 5.5 read each advice and marked which facts it used.

title: A prompt that asks before it advises: 144 conversations with six invented businesses
text:
Asking works
Compare gray and blue. Going straight to the advice, almost no conversation found the root of the problem. With five questions, Haiku found it in 14 of 24 and Sonnet in 23. The main time sink also jumps.
(The gray bar of the main time sink is generous. If someone has a hardware store, “faster quotes for builders” is right by chance, and the judge sometimes gave it the point.)

title: A prompt that asks before it advises: 144 conversations with six invented businesses
text:
The hole
Now look at the last three rows in blue. They asked a lot of things, and almost none of them about what had been tried, what can’t change or where the owner wants to go.
I searched the 240 questions for one like “what have you tried before”. There isn’t any. About half of Haiku’s had some form of how much or how many, how many orders, how many appointments, and the owner usually didn’t know.
This has a consequence you can see. The clinic had already tried automatic reminders and they had not worked. In the 16 conversations without my extra questions, automatic reminders were recommended 16 times. The workshop had signed confidentiality agreements over its clients’ logos, and after asking, both models proposed to collect the logos in a form all eight times.
None of that advice is bad. It is what anyone would say from outside, and it is what makes an owner close the laptop and say “I tried that already”.

title: A prompt that asks before it advises: 144 conversations with six invented businesses
text:
Three questions
With the three required questions, what had been tried goes from 0 to 15 with Haiku and from 5 to 19 with Sonnet. The limits go from 1 to 14 and from 0 to 19. This is how Sonnet started with the clinic, translated:

Question 1 of 5: What have you tried before to stop that leak of money, and how did it go?
Owner: Automatic message reminders for the appointments, but many older patients didn’t read them and the no-shows did not go down.

And the first recommendation was an automatic phone call instead of a message, with name, phone and time, and no medical records.
It has a price. With five questions and three already taken, there are fewer left to dig, and the root of the problem was found less: 14 to 10 and 23 to 17. I would probably allow seven. I didn’t test that. And it doesn’t always listen. Even with the answer in front of it, reminders came back in 4 of 8 conversations of the clinic, sometimes with a small change.
This is the prompt I would use:

The last part, about which decisions are mine, is my addition and I did not measure it.

title: A prompt that asks before it advises: 144 conversations with six invented businesses
text:
Limits
The owner was also a model, and sometimes it made up a detail that was not on the sheet, like a number of orders. The sheets are mine, so the questions that I found missing are the ones I had thought of. A model graded the answers. A part of them was checked by hand and mostly held, with the exception above. Six businesses are few, and a real person answers much better than a sheet.
Everything is in lab/asks-first, in Spanish, with the conversations complete. I ran the tests with help from Claude Code.

title: Calibrating a CNN on chest X-rays: how much temperature scaling fixes, and where it stops
text:
The neurologists I worked with during my thesis asked me whether they could trust the predictions of a model. Part of that question is about calibration: a model that says 90% should be right about 90 times out of 100 when it says so.
Modern networks tend to be overconfident, and the standard fix is temperature scaling (Guo et al. 2017). You divide the scores of the network by a single number, the temperature, chosen on a validation set. It does not change any prediction, only how sure the model says it is. It is one line of code and it often works very well.
I wanted to see where it stops working, with something small enough to check every number.

title: Calibrating a CNN on chest X-rays: how much temperature scaling fixes, and where it stops
text:
The setup
The data is PneumoniaMNIST (Yang et al. 2023), pediatric chest X-rays (Kermany et al. 2018) at 128 × 128 pixels, normal or pneumonia. I used the same five ResNet-18 I trained for the note on saliency maps, each with a different seed, all with a test AUC between 0.970 and 0.984.
I measured calibration with the expected calibration error (ECE, 15 bins): the average gap between how sure the model says it is and how often it is right. 0 is perfect. Each model has its own 95% bootstrap interval, and in the text I give the range over the five models.
The temperature is fitted on the 524 validation images and then used on the 624 test images.

title: Calibrating a CNN on chest X-rays: how much temperature scaling fixes, and where it stops
section: On the same kind of images
text:
On the same kind of images

Test set at 128 px, the same resolution the models were trained on.



Without correction
Temperature from validation




ECE, range over 5 models
0.075 to 0.127
0.061 to 0.121


ECE, mean

The models say 97% on average and get 88% right. Temperature scaling improves all five models, but by about one point, less than the width of the interval of each one (around ±0.02).
Looking at the errors explained why. Almost all of them go in one direction: between 61 and 108 of the 234 normal X-rays were called pneumonia, about half of those with more than 95% confidence. Of the 390 pneumonia X-rays, the models missed between 0 and 3.
And then a number I had not looked at before training: pneumonia is 74% of the training and validation sets and 62.5% of the test set. The temperature learned to correct for patients who are not the test patients.

title: Calibrating a CNN on chest X-rays: how much temperature scaling fixes, and where it stops
text:
Three checks
To see whether the problem was the method or the data it was fitted on, I tried three things on the 128 px test set:

Temperature from validation, the usual way.
A prevalence correction (Saerens et al. 2002): before the temperature, I moved the score of every X-ray by the difference between the two shares of pneumonia, in log-odds. It only uses two numbers, 74% and 62.5%, and no test labels.
An oracle: the temperature fitted on half of the test set and measured on the other half, 100 random splits. In practice you can’t do this, it needs labels from the new data, but it shows what the method can do when it sees the right data.




Calibration error on the 128 px test set with each correction. Each point is one model.


The oracle brings the error down to 0.034–0.049. The temperature it chooses is between 3.1 and 3.9, against 1.2–1.4 from validation. So the method works. What fails is fitting it on data that does not look like the test.
The prevalence correction helps half the way, down to a mean of 0.072, and also raises accuracy a little (from 0.876 to 0.887 on average). The difference in the share of pneumonia explains part of the gap, not all of it. I don’t know what else differs between the validation and test sets, and I don’t want to guess.

title: Calibrating a CNN on chest X-rays: how much temperature scaling fixes, and where it stops
text:
When the X-ray gets worse
The second test is a change of acquisition. MedMNIST has the same test X-rays stored at 64 and 28 pixels. I enlarged them back to 128 so that the model could read them, and passed them through the same models with the same temperature.



The same test X-ray stored at three resolutions.



Mean over the five models.

At 28 pixels the models were right 65% of the time and said 98%. They were not reading the X-rays anymore: they called pneumonia between 96% and 99.5% of them.



Share of test X-rays each model called pneumonia, by resolution. The dashed line is the real share, 62.5%.


Since 62.5% of the test X-rays have pneumonia, saying “pneumonia” to everything gives about 62.5% right. The accuracy at 28 px is barely above that, and the confidence went up. A temperature fitted on the original images can’t know that the images changed. This is the pattern Ovadia et al. (2019) describe for natural images under shift, and it is the one that worries me most in a hospital: the model does not say “I don’t know” when the images change, it says “I’m sure”.

title: Calibrating a CNN on chest X-rays: how much temperature scaling fixes, and where it stops
text:
What I take from it

Temperature scaling corrects what the validation set can see. If the validation set does not look like the place where the model will be used, the correction is small, and it can’t be measured without labels from that place.
Before calibrating, compare the share of each class in validation and test. It is one line of code and here it explained part of the problem.
A change of acquisition can destroy the model and leave the confidence high. You need to check the confidence on the new data, not only the accuracy.

title: Calibrating a CNN on chest X-rays: how much temperature scaling fixes, and where it stops
text:
Limits

One dataset, one architecture trained from scratch, five seeds. With 624 test images the interval of each ECE is about ±0.02.
ECE depends on the number of bins. I used 15 equal bins, as Guo et al. (2017) did.
Enlarging a 28 px image is a crude stand-in for a worse scanner. A real change of hospital moves contrast, noise and patients at the same time.
I did not try other methods (ensembles, label smoothing, recalibration on the new data). That would be the next note.

text:
Code and data
Everything is in lab/saliency: calibration.py and calibration_check.py, and the results of every model in results/, including the reliability tables I did not plot.

title: Fire Watch: I made a game to see how a decision model fails
text:
A few days ago I went to a tech event and saw a demo I kept thinking about. There was a character on the screen, you talked to it, and a panel on the side showed the probability of each thing it could do. The model never wrote a word. It only picked from a list.
They call these decision models. You give them a situation and a closed list of options, and they return one option with a number next to it. Chrome is testing an API for this, the Decisions API, and the model runs on the computer of whoever opens the page. Nothing leaves the device, which for someone who likes medical data and sensors in places without internet is a very good sentence to hear.
So I made my own game to see where it breaks.
Play Fire Watch. It works on a phone too, and you don’t need to download any model.

title: Fire Watch: I made a game to see how a decision model fails
text:
Why fire
With FIRST Global Team Colombia I work on Kawsay, a wildfire detection project. When we talked to the municipal brigades in Valle del Cauca they told us something simple: they hear about the fires too late. A phone call needs a person who already sees smoke, and the satellites pass every few hours.



The node monitoring page of the Kawsay platform, which is still a prototype. The game takes only the idea from it.


In a system like that, somebody has to read many short messages and decide what each one deserves. That is the game. Six sensors, twelve messages, and four buttons: ignore, monitor, send the drone, call the brigade. You have six flights and four trips, so you can’t send everything to everything. If you ignore smoke, you lose trees.






The brigade arrives in time.







I ignored smoke on purpose. Eleven trees.





The rule book is fixed, so every message has one right answer:



Action
When




Brigade
The camera sees smoke, whatever else happens


Drone
No smoke, 45 °C or more, and 20% humidity or less


Monitor
No smoke, and only one of those two problems


Ignore
None of them

title: Fire Watch: I made a game to see how a decision model fails
section: One event, four ways of saying it
text:
One event, four ways of saying it
I wrote 24 events, six per action, and each one in four versions. This is the same event:

Numbers. Sensor at the east gate. Temperature 47 °C. Humidity 65%. Camera: no smoke.
Spanish. Sensor en la puerta este. Temperatura 47 °C. Humedad 65 %. Cámara: sin humo.
Plain words. The battery was changed on Monday. At the east gate the air is very hot and humid as usual, and the camera shows nothing unusual.
One phrase changed. The same, but it ends with “the camera shows no smoke”.

The answer is monitor in all of them. If a model changes its mind because I changed the words, I want to know.
I tested four models. Claude Sonnet 5.5 and Claude Haiku 5.5 are general models in the cloud, and I asked them for one word. The other two ran on my MacBook (an M4): the Decisions API of Chrome 158 with its experimental flag on, and EmbeddingGemma 2, which Google offers through MediaPipe and weighs about 165 MB.

The table surprised me because the two groups fail in opposite places.
The cloud models read the numbers perfectly and Spanish made no difference. Haiku gets lost in plain words. The local models are the other way around: they do better with words and they can’t do numbers. EmbeddingGemma 2 got 6 of 24 with numbers, which is what you get with your eyes closed. When I opened the answers I saw that it had said monitor 24 times out of 24.
It makes sense once you think about what that model does. It turns the message and each option into vectors and measures which ones are close. “47 °C” and “45 °C or more” are close as text, and so are “30 °C” and “45 °C or more”. There is no place where 47 gets compared with 45.

title: Fire Watch: I made a game to see how a decision model fails
text:
The mistake was also mine
Haiku made the same error again and again: the rule book said monitor and it said ignore. In a fire system that is the bad direction.
When I looked at my own text I found a possible reason. The message said “the camera shows nothing unusual”, and my description of ignore ended with “Nothing is unusual”. I had copied my own words without noticing. In the fourth version I changed only that phrase and Haiku went from 19 or 20 to 22. The Chrome model moved one point and EmbeddingGemma 2 did not move at all, so this is a Haiku thing, at least here.
It is one phrase and 24 events, so I don’t want to make it bigger than it is. But I would look for repeated words in any product where a model chooses from a list that a person wrote.

title: Fire Watch: I made a game to see how a decision model fails
section: My first fix did not work
text:
My first fix did not work
My idea was to stop asking for the action. I would ask the local model three yes or no questions (is there smoke, is it very hot, is it very dry) and let normal code apply the rule book. I was sure about this one.
With Chrome it got worse: from 11 to 6 with numbers and from 14 to 9 with words. EmbeddingGemma 2 went from 6 to 12 with numbers, mostly because it found the smoke, and with words almost nothing changed. So I plotted the probability of each answer, one dot per event, to see what was going on.

Look at the two rows with plain words. The orange and blue dots are separated, the model does know which ones are hot and which ones are dry. The problem is the line at 0.5. For dry, every single event is above 0.7, so with that line everything is dry. And in the rows with numbers the colors are mixed, so no line would help.
Then I wrote 24 new events, different from the first ones, used them only to choose better cut points, and went back to the original 24.

From 13 to 18 with words. It is better, it is still far from 24, and with numbers it stays at 12. With Chrome, the adjusted cut points gave 11 with words, less than just asking for the action.

title: Fire Watch: I made a game to see how a decision model fails
text:
What I take from this
If I had to use a small local model for something like this, I would let the code read the thermometer, because if t >= 45 has never failed me. I would use the model for the part that only exists as language, like a neighbor’s message that says it smells like burnt leaves. And I would choose the cut points with data, since 0.5 is only a number that comes by default.
I would also try other models. EmbeddingGemma is the fastest and the weakest of the options that Chrome is considering. Resoneo tested more of them on 1,365 decisions and EmbeddingGemma also came last, at 38%, while Gemma 4 got 85%. I did not run Gemma 4 because it needs more than 4 GB, and I did not use dedicated cloud models like Gemini Decision or Jev. My median time was 55 ms per decision with Chrome, and that is the reason people care about them.
A few limits: 24 events, texts made from templates that I wrote, one run of Sonnet and one of each local model, one laptop. The API is experimental and can change next week.
Everything is in lab/fire-watch: the events, the answers (for Haiku, the last of the three runs) and the code. There is also an experiment page to run the local models in your own browser. I built the game and ran the tests with help from Claude Code. The 3D uses three.js.

title: Further pretraining did not improve masked-word prediction in clinical notes: a paired re-analysis of 101 cases
text:
In the summer of 2024 I spent some weeks at TecNM Morelia, in Mexico, with Programa Delfín. I worked with clinical notes in Spanish. There is much less of that than in English, and hospital notes have a way of writing that general models have not seen.
One part of my work was this: hide one word of a note and see if a language model can guess it. It is a first step towards removing personal details from clinical text. I took a biomedical RoBERTa for Spanish, trained it further on sets of 100, 6,000 and 10,000 notes, and wanted to see if each version got better than the one before.
The one with no extra training won.
I wrote that in my portfolio and moved on. This week I opened the notebook again, because it still had every answer of every model, 101 notes by 5 models, and I had only ever looked at the final percentage.

title: Further pretraining did not improve masked-word prediction in clinical notes: a paired re-analysis of 101 cases
text:
The notes
Before training anything I had looked at the corpus. These two plots are from the original notebook, with the colors I chose back then.






Length of the 3,001 DISTEMIST notes, in words.







The 15 diseases that appear the most.





The test was different: 101 short notes about diabetes, generated with GPT-3.5 in the style of a real case, where I masked one word by hand in each one. In 31 of them the hidden word was diabetes, so a model that always answers “diabetes” already gets 31%.

title: Further pretraining did not improve masked-word prediction in clinical notes: a paired re-analysis of 101 cases
text:
First, is it really worse

The lines are 95% intervals, and with 101 notes they are wide. They overlap almost completely. But all the models answered the same notes, so there is a better way to compare: count only the notes where they disagree, what one lost and what the other won. That is McNemar’s test.

title: Further pretraining did not improve masked-word prediction in clinical notes: a paired re-analysis of 101 cases

What changed
These are the notes where the five models do not agree.

Reading from top to bottom you can see columns flip. I went to look at the words:

The base model says dislipemia and glicemia. The trained one says dislipidemia and glucosa. And where the base model answers glucémico, the trained one answers metabólico, often very sure of itself, whether it is right or not.
It did not forget medicine. It learned another way of writing it. In most of these cases a doctor would probably read both words and not stop. (I am an engineer, so I would like one to confirm it.)

title: Further pretraining did not improve masked-word prediction in clinical notes: a paired re-analysis of 101 cases
text:
A bug in my evaluator
One note was wrong for all five models. The hidden word was cardiovascular and four of them had answered cardiovascular. The problem was mine: I took the original word from the text with its comma, so I was comparing cardiovascular with cardiovascular, and they are not equal.
It moves one point, and it was there for two years.
Then I tried a softer scorer that also accepts five groups of near synonyms that I chose by hand, like glucosa / glucemia / glicemia or glucémico / metabólico.

With that scorer the five models go from 87 to 90 out of 101, and the differences I reported are practically gone. I chose the groups after seeing the answers, which is exactly what you should not do to publish a number, so I use it only to understand where the gap was. Most of it was in my ruler.

title: Further pretraining did not improve masked-word prediction in clinical notes: a paired re-analysis of 101 cases
section: The part I did not expect
text:
The part I did not expect

Each dot is a wrong answer, and how far right it is tells how sure the model was. The base model gave more than 0.9 to one wrong answer. The models trained with 6,000 and 10,000 notes gave it to four, four and five. Accuracy looks the same and the mistakes got more confident. For something that would end up in a hospital I care more about this plot than about the first one.

title: Further pretraining did not improve masked-word prediction in clinical notes: a paired re-analysis of 101 cases
section: Why it did not improve, probably
text:
Why it did not improve, probably
When I read the training code again I found this:
folder_path = '/content/drive/MyDrive/notas_preprocesadas_100'
I trained the 100-note version with the notes after preprocessing: lowercase, no punctuation, no numbers and no stop words. And then I tested it with normal sentences. A model that learns from “paciente años diabetes tipo tratamiento” is later asked to fill a gap in a full sentence with commas. It was the only version that lost and won nothing, which fits. I only have the path of that one in the notebook, so I can’t say it for the others.
I was also cutting each note at 256 tokens. More than a quarter of the notes have over 600 words, so the model never saw the end of the long ones.

title: Further pretraining did not improve masked-word prediction in clinical notes: a paired re-analysis of 101 cases
text:
If I did it again
I would train on the text as it is. I would decide before starting how many test notes I need to see a difference of, say, five points, and 101 is not enough. I would have two people agree on which words count as the same before looking at any answer. And I would plot the confidence of the mistakes from the first day.
The 505 answers are in lab/clinical-words (only the hidden word and the prediction, not the notes). The project is here and the code is in its repository.

title: A vague discount rule and 1,200 quotes: what three models decided
text:
In small companies a lot of rules live in someone’s head. How much discount, for whom, who pays the shipping. It works while that person answers every message, and it stops working the day you ask an assistant to make the quotes.
I wanted to see what a model does with a rule that is half written. I expected a mess, with a different price every time. That is not what happened.

title: A vague discount rule and 1,200 quotes: what three models decided
text:
The test
I invented a coffee roaster with four products and ten orders, five from old clients and five from new ones. Everything was in Spanish. This was the vague policy, translated:

We give discounts for large orders, normally between 5 and 10%, depending on the client. With the shops that have been with us for a while we try to help a bit more. Shipping is charged depending on the case. If the order is good, sometimes we cover it. A normal shipping is more or less $25,000.

And this was the written one: 0% below $1,500,000, 5% from there, 10% from $3,000,000, nothing else. Shipping is $25,000 below $1,000,000 and free above.
I asked three models for each quote ten times, in four ways:

With the vague policy, and permission to ask the owner.
With the vague policy, and the client waiting for a total.
With the written rule.
The model only reads the order, and a program applies the rule.

That makes 1,200 answers.

I liked the first column. Almost always the model stopped and asked something like this, which is an answer of Sonnet, translated:

What discount (between 5 and 10%) applies to Tienda Azafrán for this order (subtotal $1,992,000), and do we charge the shipping (approx. $25,000) or cover it?

Those questions are the list of decisions that the owner had not made. You could copy them, answer each one once, and you would have the policy.

title: A vague discount rule and 1,200 quotes: what three models decided
text:
Without permission, they decide
The only thing I changed was the ending. “The client is waiting. What total do we send?”

All of them answered, 300 times out of 300. And they did not answer at random. Old clients got 10% and new clients got 5%, in 298 of the 300 quotes, with three different models.
Nobody wrote that rule. It is a possible reading of my text, since I did say that old clients get a bit more help. But the policy talked about large orders, and the size did not matter at all. An order of $456,000, the smallest one, got 5%. The largest one, of $4,296,000, got the same 5%. An old client with $846,000 got 10%.
The shipping is the part that did change. For the same order, some answers charged it and some gave it away.
I checked the arithmetic and it was right the 300 times. That worries me more than if it was wrong, because if you review these quotes you find nothing. The totals add up, and they even look consistent.

title: A vague discount rule and 1,200 quotes: what three models decided
section: What I would do with this
text:
What I would do with this
I would write the rule before choosing the tool. If it fits in one line, like “5% from a million and a half”, it does not need AI at all, and it can live in a spreadsheet.
I would always leave the model a way out, with a field for its question. It costs one line and it was the difference between asking 290 times out of 300 and never asking.
And I would keep the questions it asks in the first week. They are a good draft of what I call the house book, everything you would explain to a new person on the first day.

title: A vague discount rule and 1,200 quotes: what three models decided
text:
Limits
The company is invented and the orders are clean. The old client was always written as “client since 2022”, and that probably pushed the models to use it. I tested three models of the same family. And the vague policy mentions 5 and 10, so a different text would give a different invented rule. What I would expect to find again is that there is one.
The code and the 1,200 answers are in lab/same-quote. I ran the tests with help from Claude Code.

title: Let the model read and a program add: 40 documents with three models
text:
At work we built a platform for accountants that helps them file a local business tax in Colombia. Every municipality writes its own rules, with its rates, its penalties and its calendar, and they change. The accountant has to read the municipal agreement, go through the documents of the client and fill in a form line by line. One wrong figure is a fine. (I am an engineer and not an accountant, and everything below comes from that.)
The rule we follow is that AI reads and proposes, a program calculates, and an accountant approves. Nothing goes out without that approval.
You could think this is too much trouble, if the model can read the document and give you the total in one go. It is a fair doubt, because models have improved a lot since that rule was written. So I put it to the test.

title: Let the model read and a program add: 40 documents with three models
text:
The town that doesn’t exist
I invented a town with five activities and their rates, a signage tax of 15%, a fire brigade surcharge of 3%, withholdings and a discount for paying early. It does not match any real place and it is useless for filing anything. With that I generated 40 documents in Spanish. This is one of them, translated:

Activity 412, consulting, closed with income of $436,996,994, no returns. Retail, code 203: $343,928,131, of which $6,010,663 were returned. Payroll for the last quarter was $41,780,000. Clients withheld $346,559. They will pay within the early payment period.

Each one has a trap, a figure that is not needed, like that payroll.
I tried two ways with three models of different sizes. In the first, the model gets the document and the rules and answers with the total. In the second, the model only pulls the data into a JSON, and a program of ten lines does the math:
tax     = thousands(sum((income - returns) * rate / 1000))
signage = thousands(tax * 0.15)
fire    = thousands(tax * 0.03)
total   = tax + signage + fire - thousands(withheld)
if early_payment:
    total = total - thousands(total * 0.10)

title: Let the model read and a program add: 40 documents with three models
text:
What happened

The three models read the 40 documents without a single mistake. Not one figure changed, and none of them fell for the trap. With the program doing the math, the three got 40 out of 40.
When the model does everything, the smallest one gets 21 out of 40, the middle one 37 and the big one 40.
I leave that last 40 here because it goes against my rule and it would be easy to hide. Sonnet 5.5 did the math 40 times in a row and never failed. So “models can’t add” is no longer a good reason for the rule.

title: Let the model read and a program add: 40 documents with three models
text:
What the mistakes look like

Most of them are one thousand pesos: a rounding done too early or too late. Those are the hardest to see, because the total looks a lot like the right one. But a form that is off by a thousand pesos is wrong.
And there is one that is something else. The document I showed above gives $6,647,000. The small model answered $4,174,000. That is almost two and a half million pesos less, in one of the shortest documents, said as calmly as all the others. If you review a sample of ten, that one will probably not be there.

title: Let the model read and a program add: 40 documents with three models
text:
So why the program
If the big model always gets it right, I am left with three reasons.
The first one is that you can check the program. It is ten lines, and an accountant can read them with me and say “that is not how it’s rounded here”. I can’t ask a model that got 40 right what it is going to do with number 41.
The second is that when something goes wrong you know where. If the figure is wrong, the model read it wrong. If the figure is right and the total is not, the rule is wrong. If both are right and something else was filed, someone approved without looking. When one model does the three steps, you can’t have that conversation.
The third is that with the program the small model is enough. Pulling the data is easier than doing the math, and in my test it was also faster: with Haiku 4.5, about 4 seconds to read against 14 to read and calculate. For many companies that decides if the project pays for itself.

title: Let the model read and a program add: 40 documents with three models
text:
Taking it to another process
One way of repeating this in another company is to take the process and mark each step with a letter. R for reading, summarizing or classifying. C for calculating or applying a rule that is already written. D for deciding something that somebody answers for.
With this case: reading the municipal agreement is R, pulling the client’s figures is R, calculating the tax is C, approving is D. The R steps are good to start with AI. The C steps almost always want a program, and sometimes it already exists and lives in a spreadsheet. The D steps stay with a person who has a name and a position.
You can do it on paper in one meeting, and then the conversation does not start with the tool.

title: Let the model read and a program add: 40 documents with three models
text:
What this test doesn’t say
A program generated the documents, so they are clean. A real one comes scanned, crooked, with a handwritten note on the side, and there the reading will fail. The rules fit in one paragraph, and a municipal agreement has dozens of pages. I ran each model once. Reading 40 of my documents perfectly does not mean reading your client’s perfectly, and that is why the accountant is still at the end.
The code, the 40 documents and all the answers are in lab/ia-propone (in Spanish).
